items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: Even for example the greatest classic Miles Davis Quintet, like Red Garland, Philly Jo, Coltrane, Paul Chambers. The people did not come.

ctx.x: That’s an interesting statement. I mean you certainly made an impact and kept that tradition alive. You know when you read about your music, most people mention that it brings in a whole other area of influence from your native culture. And when you write do you consciously try to think of things from your youth that are now combined with American jazz, or is it just kind of part of you?

No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died. Before that, you know it was just a Japanese traditional concept, or being Japanese playing jazz was some sort of a handicap. When I was growing up in Japan as a player, they always said that Filipino people have better feeling than Japanese, and indeed the Filipino players played better than us, and it’s simply because they have a longer history. They weren’t under — they were colonized by America so they are more exposed for jazz, much longer than…

butter.” The smell of butter means very American. Because butter is western. Japanese traditionally, we have no butter. So they used to say her playing smells of butter. That’s what they used to say. So that has been going on for a long time. When Duke Ellington died, it was ’73, or ’74 I think, and there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir. And he was talking about that fact that Duke was, how proud he was about his race. And he was pointing out so many music was based on his race, which I knew some…

items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Well, the first time I heard of Coltrane was in Los Angeles. And uh, with Miles‟ group with … that was the first time I heard, uh…

ctx.x: So it was Beethoven‟s music? Was it the particular way of playing it? Or just the sound or both?

No, I think it was Beethoven‟s music. His music was … it‟s not quite … you know, I don‟t think [at] that particular time I didn‟t think anything the way I‟m analyzing today. Beethoven‟s music is more … [to] some degree, I think—this is probably a far- out analysis—but Coltrane, like, compared to Sonny Rollins … Sonny Rollins, if it was everyone like that, you might as well forget about it, or something. Certain things, Beethoven had certain things, more, try harder kind of things. Mozart, on the other hand, is…
Did you finish high school before your family emigrated to Japan?
